stem:
Moyo's Hardware, Gweru, is owned by Tendai Moyo. The financial year ends on 31 December 2025. The rent payments of US\$5,980 made during 2025 included January and February 2026.

| Item | Paid or received in 2025 (US\$) | At 1 January 2025 | At 31 December 2025 |
| --- | ---: | --- | --- |
| Rent (US\$460 a month) | 5,980 | 460 prepaid | to be calculated |
| Wages | 41,600 | 1,240 owing | 1,560 owing |
| Insurance (annual premium paid on 1 July 2025 covering the twelve months to 30 June 2026) | 3,600 | 1,710 prepaid | to be calculated |
| Commission received | 2,960 | 180 accrued | 270 accrued |

Trade receivables (debtors) in the ledger at 31 December 2025, before any adjustment, were US\$39,200. The following adjustments are to be made:

- Bad debts of US\$900 and US\$650 are to be written off.
- Bad debts of US\$250 previously written off were recovered in December and credited to bad debts recovered.
- The allowance for doubtful debts is to be 5% of the remaining trade receivables. The allowance account had a balance of US\$1,170 at 1 January 2025.

Use the income statement as the name for the statement of profit and loss.

parts.label: (i)
parts.stem: Calculate the rent prepaid at 31 December 2025.
parts.explanation: January and February 2026 are two months: 2 × 460 = 920.
parts.workedSolution: 1. January and February 2026 are two months: 2 × 460 = 920.

parts.label: (ii)
parts.stem: Calculate the rent expense for 2025.

parts.stem: Where is the accrued wages of US\$1,560 shown in the statement of financial position?

options.rationale: Correct: it is owed at the year end.
That heading is for amounts prepaid or owed to the business.
Accruals are liabilities, not deductions from capital.

parts.explanation: An accrued expense is a current liability.

parts.stem: Insurance

parts.label: (i)
parts.stem: Calculate the insurance prepaid at 31 December 2025.
parts.explanation: The premium covers 12 months to 30 June 2026; six months (January to June 2026) are prepaid: 3,600 × 6/12 = 1,800.
parts.workedSolution: 1. The premium covers 12 months to 30 June 2026; six months (January to June 2026) are prepaid: 3,600 × 6/12 = 1,800.

parts.label: (ii)
parts.stem: Calculate the insurance expense for 2025.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Calculate the commission received to be credited to the income statement for 2025.

parts.stem: Bad debts and the allowance

parts.stem: Calculate the trade receivables remaining after the write-offs.

parts.label: (ii)

parts.label: (iv)
parts.stem: Calculate the total bad debts expense in the income statement: write-offs, less the recovery, plus the increase in the allowance.

parts.label: (g)
parts.stem: Explain how the matching concept is applied when an accrual for wages is made.

points.description: Wages are charged to the year in which the staff worked, not the year of payment
The unpaid amount is shown as a liability so profit is not overstated

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The staff worked in 2025, so their wages are an expense of 2025 even though they are paid in 2026. The unpaid amount is shown as a liability, so profit is not overstated.

stem:
Tafara and Farai run a bakery in Masvingo as a partnership. They share profits and losses equally and each has capital of US\$45,000. They want to open a second bakery and need US\$160,000. They are considering forming a private limited company with ordinary shares of US\$1 each. The two founders would take 90,000 shares in exchange for the partnership's capital, and the company would start with reserves of US\$20,000.

They have two ways to raise the US\$160,000:

- **Option 1:** issue 10% loan notes of US\$160,000.
- **Option 2:** issue 160,000 new ordinary shares of US\$1 at par to outside investors.

Expected profit before interest for the new business is US\$64,000 a year.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Suppose the business fails, with assets that realise US\$104,000 and debts of US\$158,000.

parts.label: (i)
parts.stem: Calculate the shortfall owed to creditors.

parts.label: (ii)
parts.stem: As a partnership, calculate the amount each partner would have to find from private assets (equal shares).

parts.label: (iii)
parts.stem: As a private company with fully paid shares, calculate the amount each shareholder must contribute towards the shortfall.
parts.explanation: Nil. Shareholders' liability is limited to the amount unpaid on their shares.
parts.workedSolution: 1. Nil. Shareholders' liability is limited to the amount unpaid on their shares.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Which of the following is a feature of a private limited company?

options.content: Its shares are not offered to the public
options.rationale: Correct: this distinguishes it from a public company.

options.content: It ends when a shareholder dies
options.rationale: A company continues in spite of changes of shareholders.

options.content: It is not a separate legal person
options.rationale: A company is a separate legal person.

parts.explanation: A private company may not offer shares to the public.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Option 1: loan notes

parts.label: (i)
parts.stem: Calculate the annual interest on the loan notes.

parts.label: (ii)
parts.stem: Calculate the gearing ratio (non-current liabilities ÷ (share capital + reserves + non-current liabilities)) as a percentage to one decimal place.

parts.label: (iii)
parts.stem: Calculate the interest cover (profit before interest ÷ interest), to one decimal place.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Under Option 2, calculate the percentage of the votes held by each founder (one vote per share; each founder holds 45,000 shares), to one decimal place.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Advise the partners which option to choose. Use the figures you have calculated and refer to control, risk and cost.

points.description: Option 1 costs interest of 16,000 a year, which leaves profit before tax of 48,000 and must be paid even in a poor year
Gearing of 59.3% is high, so lenders and the business carry greater risk; interest cover of 4.0 times is reasonable
Option 2 has no fixed commitment and gearing of nil, so is safer in a poor year
Option 2 reduces each founder to 18% of the votes (36% together), so control is diluted and new shareholders share dividends
A reasoned recommendation, such as Option 1 if profits are stable and control is important, otherwise Option 2

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Option 1 keeps full control with the founders but costs 16,000 a year in interest, leaving 48,000 of profit before tax. Gearing would be 59.3%, which is high, although interest cover of 4.0 times shows the interest is affordable. Option 2 avoids fixed payments and leaves gearing at nil, but the founders' votes fall to 36% together and profits are shared. If the profits are stable and the partners want control I would advise Option 1; if they fear a poor year Option 2 is safer.

parts.explanation: One mark per point; the recommendation must be consistent with the figures.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: Explain why the partners may wish to become a limited company.

points.description: Limited liability protects their private assets if the business fails
The company is a separate legal entity and continues if an owner leaves or dies
Shares can be issued to raise capital from outside investors

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: A company gives them limited liability, so their private assets are safe if the business fails. It is a separate legal entity that continues when an owner leaves, and it can issue shares to raise capital.

explanation: This item tests the forms of business and the choice of long-term finance.
hints: Limited liability means shareholders do not pay the shortfall from private assets.
Gearing = loan notes ÷ (shares + reserves + loan notes).
